x.s: Every quote you get for an AI agent is one number, and that number hides two different things.

One is calculable to the cent, today, from published pricing pages. The other has no public benchmark anywhere, and anybody giving you an industry average for it made it up. So this article splits AI agent development cost in half: the running cost with the arithmetic done, and an honest account of what moves the build price.
The running number is usually the surprise. It is smaller than people fear on model costs and larger than people expect on platform metering.
Running cost, part one: the model
This is the bill from whoever makes the model. It is per token, published, and the part everyone worries about unnecessarily. Pricing per million tokens, September 2026:

Two levers cut that materially. Anthropic's Batch API is 50% off input and output, and prompt caching reads cost 0.1 times the input rate, which matters for an agent resending the same instructions on every call. OpenAI publishes cached input at roughly a tenth of standard. Google's batch discount is also 50%, and its priority tier costs an 80% premium.
The dated cost cliff you should budget for now
Google's Gemini 3.8 and 3.7 Flash prices are
promotional through 31 December 2026
and
double on 1 January 2027

, going to $1.50 input and $7.50 output. If you are building a business case on Flash pricing for next year, use the post promotional numbers. This published cliff will quietly break a lot of spreadsheets.
Running cost, part two: the platform, which is where it actually hurts
Agent platforms do not bill per token. They bill per action, and their unit of counting is where the surprise lives.
Zapier Agents
offers a
free tier at 400 activities a month and Pro at $33.33 a month billed annually
, $400 a year, for up to 1,500 activities. The definition is the important bit: activities include actions the agent takes, plus
browsing the web
and
looking up attached knowledge
. Both burn an activity.
So an agent that researches before it acts might spend three or four activities on one useful outcome. At 1,500 a month, that is closer to 400 real outcomes than 1,500.
Microsoft Copilot Studio
is the clearest metering arithmetic in the category. It charges
$0.01 per Copilot Credit
on pay as you go, billed in arrears:
Source:
Microsoft Copilot Studio message and credit management
Work one real interaction: a generative answer plus one agent action is 7 credits, so
7 cents
. Ten thousand interactions a month is
about $700 a month

, before a dollar of model API cost. Agents get disabled at 125% of prepaid capacity, so budget deliberately rather than discovering the ceiling on a Monday. Compare that $700 against the model table and you can see where an agent's running cost really comes from.
The cost nobody puts in the quote: agents loop
This is what makes agent economics different from ordinary automation, and it comes from the people who make the models. Anthropic's
Building Effective Agents
defines an agent as a system where the model "dynamically direct[s] their own processes and tool usage", and describes them plainly as "LLMs using tools based on environmental feedback in a loop."
In a loop. That is the cost.

A deterministic workflow makes one model call per run because a developer wrote the path. An agent makes as many calls as it decides it needs: read the request, pick a tool, look at the result, decide whether that was enough, try again. Nobody can tell you the number in advance, because deciding the number is the agent's job.

Anthropic states the tradeoff directly: "Agentic systems often trade latency and cost for better task performance, and you should consider when this tradeoff makes sense." And more bluntly: "The autonomous nature of agents means higher costs, and the potential for compounding errors."

So multiply your per interaction model cost by a loop factor, and remember the platform meters every one of those tool calls too. Looping plus per action billing is why agent bills come in above the estimate. Our
AI automation cost breakdown
covers the same metering problem for non agent workflows, where the numbers are friendlier.
What AI agent development cost actually depends on

Now the honest part. There is no credible published benchmark for what a US small business pays to have an AI agent built. No federal survey, no representative study, nothing. Any article quoting "$15,000 to $50,000 for a custom AI agent" is reading one agency's rate card and calling it a market.
I am not going to add another invented range. Here is what genuinely moves the price.
How many systems have to talk to each other.
One system with a good API is a small job. Four, one of them a legacy tool with a CSV export and no API, is a different job.
Whether your process is written down.

This moves the number more than the technology does. A builder working from a documented process prices a known task. One working from "we sort of just know how it goes" prices discovery, and discovery is where estimates go wrong.
How much scaffolding the agent needs.
Anthropic's own
shop experiment
went from losing money to profitable mainly by adding a CRM, costed inventory data, price comparison and an oversight agent. That scaffolding is the build. The
deployment guide for support agents
shows it in practice.
What the reliability bar is.
An agent drafting internal summaries needs far less testing than one touching customer money. Evaluation and guardrail work scales with consequence, not complexity.
Who maintains it.
APIs change, prices change, and somebody owns the thing after launch. If that is not in the arrangement it becomes awkward in month four.
For scale, Gartner puts enterprise generative AI deployment approaches at
$5M to $20M
. That is nowhere near your number, but it does explain why quotes in this space spread so wide.
The test for whether you need an agent at all
Run this before you price anything. It takes ten minutes and saves a lot of money.
Write the process down step by step. Then ask:
can I write the sequence in advance?

If yes, you want a workflow, not an agent. It costs one model call instead of ten, it can meter as one run instead of many actions, it fails predictably, and you can debug it. Anthropic's own guidance is to find "the simplest solution possible, and only increasing complexity when needed", and that workflows "offer predictability and consistency" while agents suit cases where flexibility is genuinely needed at scale.

If the sequence genuinely varies every time, based on things you cannot enumerate, an agent earns its cost. That is a real category, and a smaller one than the marketing suggests. Most of what gets sold as an agent is a workflow with better branding.
How to sanity check an AI agent development cost quote

Calculate the running cost first, because you can, and because it tells you within an hour whether the idea clears its own bar. Steps times runs times loop factor, against your platform's unit. If the answer is $700 a month to handle work costing $400 in staff time, you have your answer and you did not spend anything to get it.

Then treat the build as what it is: mostly integration and mostly your own process documentation. The businesses that get good prices arrive with the process written down, and that is something you can do yourself over a weekend.

So: are AI agents replacing SaaS? They are replacing specific tasks inside SaaS tools and almost nothing else, and the data is public and fairly blunt. Under a fifth of small US firms use AI at all. Gartner expects more than 40% of agentic AI projects to be cancelled by the end of 2027. And the biggest research lab in the space published a guide telling you to use the simplest thing that works.
What follows is the definition that matters, the four things people call agents, and what the adoption numbers show once you separate the firm from the employee.
What an AI agent actually is, according to the people building them
The most useful definition comes from Anthropic's engineering team, in
Building Effective Agents
, published December 2024. They split the category in two.
Workflows
are "systems where LLMs and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths." A developer wrote the sequence. The model fills in the parts that need language.
Agents
are "systems where LLMs dynamically direct their own processes and tool usage, maintaining control over how they accomplish tasks." Nobody wrote the sequence. The model picks the next step each time.
They put it more plainly elsewhere in the same piece: "Agents are typically just LLMs using tools based on environmental feedback in a loop."
That distinction is the spine of this whole question, because almost everything sold as an agent in 2026 is a workflow. OpenAI's
practical guide to building agents
draws the same line from the other side: applications that integrate a language model "but don't use them to control workflow execution" are, in their words, "not agents".
Anthropic is also not shy about the tradeoff. "The autonomous nature of agents means higher costs, and the potential for compounding errors." That is the model vendor saying it.
The four things people call agents
Four genuinely different technologies wear one word. Here is the split the primary sources support.

IBM's framing is the quickest way to remember it: "AI assistants are reactive, performing tasks at your request", while "AI agents are primarily proactive." A chatbot in your help widget is not an agent. Neither is a Zap that summarises an email. Both are useful. Neither replaces software.
Are AI agents replacing SaaS tools, or replacing tasks inside them
Software as a service is mostly three things bundled together: a database of your records, a set of workflows around that database, and an interface for humans to look at both.

Agents are currently decent at the third thing and part of the second. They can read a record, draft a reply, classify an enquiry, pull structured data out of a document and put it somewhere. That is real value. It is also the top layer, not the foundation.

The database underneath is not going anywhere, because an agent needs somewhere to write. What actually happens is that the interface gets thinner and the agent does more of the clicking. Your CRM stays. The half hour you spent updating it goes. That is a good outcome and it is not replacement.
What the adoption data actually says
The best source on US business AI adoption is the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, because it is a real federal survey with a published question, not a vendor poll.

Two things jump out. Most firms are not using AI in producing goods or services at all, and small firms showed no significant change between December 2025 and May 2026 while larger firms rose. More revealing, adoption among adopters is shallow: roughly 57% use it in three or fewer business functions, led by sales and marketing at 52%.

That is not a market where software is being replaced. That is a market where a fifth of businesses have started using a new tool for one or two jobs. The same paper notes that AI related employment decreases occur in only 2% of firms, and 66% of adopters use AI to augment rather than replace work.
What the vendor data says, and the phrase "agent washing"
Gartner published two numbers in June 2025 that belong in every conversation about this.
The first:
over 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027
, "due to escalating costs, unclear business value or inadequate risk controls."
The second should change how you shop. Of the thousands of vendors claiming to sell agentic AI, Gartner estimates only around
130 are genuine

. The rest are what Gartner calls agent washing: rebranding assistants, RPA and chatbots. Analyst Anushree Verma put it directly: "Most agentic AI projects right now are early stage experiments or proof of concepts that are mostly driven by hype and are often misapplied."
Roughly 130 real ones out of thousands. If a tool promises to replace a category of software, the base rate says it probably does not do what the homepage says.
The 2029 prediction, and the word doing all the work
The optimistic Gartner number gets quoted constantly, usually wrong. The actual prediction, from March 2025, is that
by 2029 agentic AI will autonomously resolve 80% of common customer service issues
without human intervention, with a 30% reduction in operational costs.
The load bearing word is
common

Not 80% of customer service issues. Eighty percent of the common ones: password resets, order status checks, refund windows. Exactly the bounded, verifiable, repetitive tasks agents are already reasonable at. The hard tickets, the angry ones, the ones where policy meets judgement, are not in that number. Anyone quoting it as "AI will handle 80% of customer service" has dropped the only word that made it a careful forecast.
If you are actually planning that deployment, our guide to
deploying an AI agent for customer support
covers what to automate first and what to keep human.
What this means for what you buy this year
Stop asking whether agents will replace your stack. Ask which specific task inside your stack is bounded enough that a wrong answer is cheap and a human sees the output before it matters.

Then check whether it needs an agent at all. Anthropic's guidance is to find "the simplest solution possible, and only increasing complexity when needed". A deterministic workflow that runs identically every time is cheaper, faster and vastly easier to debug, and the right starting point for most businesses. Price it before you commit, because agents loop, which is why
AI agent running costs
behave differently from ordinary automation billing.
So, are AI agents replacing SaaS or not
The honest read of the data is that we are early. Not that agents are fake, and not that they are about to eat your software. Somewhere in between, which makes for a bad headline and a better plan.

The businesses getting value are doing unglamorous things. They picked one repetitive task, wrapped it in checks, put a person on the output, and left the rest alone. Nobody writes a thread about that. It works.

items.a: No, not at the tool level. They absorb specific tasks inside those tools: drafting, classifying, summarising, data entry. The record system stays, because the agent needs somewhere to read from and write to. Census data shows under 20% of the smallest US firms use AI at all, which is not the profile of a market mid replacement.

items.a: Who decides the next step. Anthropic defines workflows as systems where models and tools run through predefined code paths, and agents as systems where the model directs its own process and tool use. A workflow is predictable and cheap. An agent is flexible and costs more, with a real risk of compounding errors.

items.a: Ask what the agent does when its first approach fails. A real agent picks a different tool and tries again. A rebranded workflow errors out. items.a: Not wait, but start narrow. The evidence supports agents on bounded, verifiable tasks where a human reviews the output, and does not yet support long unsupervised chains. Pick one process, run it for a month, and measure it. That is a far better use of a quarter than a platform migration.

It has to do with how your platform counts.

That is the part that catches people. You compare subscription prices, you pick the cheap one, and four months later the bill has quadrupled because the tool you chose charges you per step and you built something with eight steps. Below are the actual published numbers as of September 2026, where the money really goes, and how to work out your own figure before you commit to anything.
The three things you are actually paying for
Most articles on this treat AI automation as one line item. It is three, and they behave completely differently.
The platform.
The thing that connects your apps and runs the sequence. Zapier, Make, n8n. This is a predictable monthly subscription plus usage.
The model.
If any step involves an AI actually reading, writing or deciding something, you pay per token to whoever makes the model. This is pure usage and it is usually smaller than people fear.
The build.
Somebody has to design and wire the thing. That is either your weekend or someone's invoice.
The first two are published and you can calculate them today. The third is the one where quotes vary wildly, and I will get to why.

The metering trap, and the one calculation that saves you money
Zapier's own help documentation is clear about what it charges for: "A task is any successful action that runs in Zapier. Only successful actions count toward your task usage."

n8n's documentation is equally clear, and says something completely different: "An execution is a single run of your entire workflow. It doesn't matter how many steps are in the workflow or how much data it processes. It's still a single execution."
Now run the same automation through both.

Say you build something ordinary. A form comes in, the lead gets checked against your CRM, created if new, tagged, assigned to someone, a Slack message fires, a confirmation email goes out, and a row lands in a reporting sheet. That is eight actions. Say it runs 2,000 times a month, which is a busy but not enormous small business.
On Zapier that is
16,000 tasks
. On n8n it is
2,000 executions
, which sits inside the €20 Starter plan. Self hosted, it is your server bill and nothing else.
Same automation. Same volume. Wildly different invoice.

This is why "what does automation cost" has no single answer, and why the honest version of the question is "what shape is your automation, and does your platform charge for shape or for runs?" A few automations that each do a lot of steps punish you on Zapier. A lot of automations that each do very little are fine anywhere.
One more thing worth knowing about Make specifically: it now bills in
credits

, not the "operations" that every comparison table online still describes, and its own pricing page notes that "some advanced features leveraging Make's AI Provider may use more" than one credit per action. So an AI flavoured scenario burns quota faster than the same scenario built on plain connectors. If you read a Make cost comparison written before this year, the units in it are wrong.

I am not going to invent an industry average, because no credible survey of what US small businesses pay for automation builds exists. What I can tell you is what drives the number: how many systems have to talk to each other, whether they have decent APIs, and how much of your process is written down before anyone starts. That last one moves the price more than the technology does.
What to do before you spend anything
Count the steps in the process you want to automate. Actually count them, on paper.
Multiply by how many times a month it runs. That gives you your task number, and you can price Zapier against n8n directly instead of guessing.

Then ask the harder question: does this process need an AI in it at all, or does it just need to be connected? Anthropic's own engineering guidance says to find "the simplest solution possible, and only increasing complexity when needed", and warns that "the autonomous nature of agents means higher costs, and the potential for compounding errors". A deterministic workflow that runs the same way every time is cheaper, faster and easier to debug than an agent, and for a large share of small business tasks it is also the correct answer.
Start with one process. The boring one that everybody in the business complains about. Price it, build it, watch it for a month, then decide whether the second one is worth it.
The honest summary

Running the automation is cheap. Almost always cheaper than people expect, and often under $100 a month for a small business doing real volume. The expensive parts are choosing a platform whose billing model fights your workload, and building something complicated before you have written down what the simple version was supposed to do.

If you want to work out your own number, the calculation in this article is genuinely all of it: steps, times runs, against your platform's unit. Ten minutes with a piece of paper will tell you more than any quote.

items.q: Is Zapier or n8n cheaper for a small business?
items.a: It depends entirely on the shape of your automations. Zapier charges per successful action, so an eight step workflow costs eight tasks each time it runs. n8n charges per execution, so the same workflow costs one. If you run a small number of long workflows, n8n is dramatically cheaper. If you run many very short ones, the gap narrows a lot.

items.q: Can I run AI automation for free?
items.a: Partly. n8n's Community Edition has no licence fee and you pay only for the server you run it on. Zapier and Make both have free tiers, at 100 tasks and 1,000 credits a month respectively, which is enough to test an idea but not to run a business on. Model API usage is never free at volume, though for light workloads it costs cents.

items.q: How much does an AI agent cost compared to normal automation?
items.a: Meaningfully more, in both directions. Agent platforms meter more aggressively, Copilot Studio charges 5 credits per agent action against 2 for a generative answer, and agents make more model calls per outcome because they loop. Anthropic's guidance is explicit that agentic systems trade cost and latency for flexibility, so only pay for one where the flexibility is the point.

x.s: Two statistics show up in almost every AI consulting pitch deck in America right now. One misquotes an eight year old prediction about something else. The other comes from a survey where most respondents had never tried the thing being measured.
If a consultant opens with either, you have learned something about them for free.

This covers the AI consulting cost for small business owners in the terms that matter: what drives the price, what a real engagement should produce, and how to sort a serious advisor from someone reselling a webinar. First the statistics audit.
The statistics audit, or how to check your consultant in ninety seconds
The one about 85 percent of AI projects failing
You will hear that Gartner found 85 percent of AI projects fail, cited as a failure rate to justify hiring somebody. Here is the actual source. Gartner, press release,
13 February 2018
. The exact wording:
> "Gartner predicts that through 2022, 85 percent of AI projects will deliver erroneous outcomes > due to bias in data, algorithms or the teams responsible for managing them."
Read it twice. It is not a failure rate, not about return on investment, and not about pilots reaching production. It is a prediction about
bias producing erroneous outcomes
, and its window closed in

So every 2026 article citing it quotes an eight year old forecast about a different subject, whose timeframe expired four years ago, and relabels it as a failure statistic. That is not a paraphrase. It is a different claim.
The one about 95 percent of AI pilots failing
This one is newer and gets shared harder: the claim that MIT found 95 percent of AI pilots fail.

The source is a July 2025 MIT NANDA working paper, "The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business 2025". It says "just 5% of integrated AI pilots are extracting millions in value, while the vast majority remain stuck with no measurable P&L impact." The methodology is where it falls apart:

items.s: 153 survey responses
, 52 structured interviews, plus a review of public initiatives
Labelled
preliminary findings
, and
not peer reviewed
Roughly
80% of surveyed companies had never piloted custom AI at all
The success bar was "marked and sustained" improvement within six months
All four authors were commercializing agentic AI frameworks

x.s: That third point is the killer. If four fifths of your sample never attempted a pilot, a statistic about pilots failing has the wrong denominator. It conflates never tried with tried and failed, and at n=153 the 5% success figure may rest on two or three companies.

The defensible version: a non peer reviewed MIT NANDA working paper based on 153 survey responses reported that only 5% of integrated AI pilots produced measurable P&L impact within six months, a figure widely misreported as a project failure rate.
Why this matters when you are hiring
A consultant who opens with either has not checked their own sources. That is a fair proxy for how they will treat the numbers in your business case.
There is plenty of real, sourced pessimism available. Gartner predicts
over 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027
due to escalating costs, unclear business value or inadequate risk controls, and estimates only about 130 of thousands of agentic AI vendors are genuine. That is dated and attributable.

The gap that explains everything

Under 20% of small firms use AI. Fifty percent of small business workers use AI. Both are real and correctly measured. They differ because they ask different people different questions. The Census asks a firm officer whether the business used AI in producing goods or services. The Chamber, through an Ipsos KnowledgePanel sample of 1,070 workers at businesses of 2 to 499 employees fielded in May 2026, asks workers about any use at work.
So most small business AI adoption in America is
an employee quietly using ChatGPT
, not a company deploying anything. A consultant citing one of those numbers without saying which level it measures is either confused or hoping you are.
The 6% figure
The most striking number in the Chamber data is the purpose split. Of small business workers using AI: 64% for personal productivity, 26% for recurring tasks, and only
6% for workflow automation
Six percent. That is the honest size of both the opportunity and the gap. Almost nobody has connected AI to the actual flow of work. Our
AI automation cost breakdown
covers what closing that gap costs to run.
The AI consulting cost for small business owners, and what drives it

I will not publish a price here. A headline day rate tells you nothing useful, and there is no credible survey of what US small businesses pay for AI consulting. Anybody quoting a market average is quoting themselves. Here is what drives the number.
Scope of assessment.
One process is a small piece of work. Mapping every process across three departments is not.
How many systems are involved, and whether they have APIs.
Two modern tools that talk to each other is straightforward. A legacy system exporting only a CSV is not.
Whether anything gets built.
Advice is priced differently from implementation. Be clear which you are buying, because the two get quoted together and only one gets delivered.
How much of your process is documented.

This moves price more than the technology does. A consultant working from written processes prices a known job. One working from a conversation prices discovery, and discovery is where estimates go wide.
The reliability bar.
Anything touching customer money or regulated data needs testing and guardrails. Those hours are real.
Whether ongoing support is included.
Prices change, APIs change. Ask who owns the thing in month six.

Then they published all of it. Which is why it is the best case study in existence for anyone working out how to deploy AI agents for customer support, and why I would rather point you at Anthropic's failures than a vendor's demo.
Here is the practical version: what to automate first, what to keep human, what scaffolding changed the outcome, and a rollout sequence you can follow without betting your customers on a demo.
What to automate first
There is a shape of task current agents genuinely do well, and it has four properties. It is
bounded
, with a clear finish line. It is
verifiable
, so you can tell from the output whether it worked. It is
tool mediated
, so the agent reads and writes through an API rather than guessing. And a wrong answer is
cheap
, because a human sees it first. In a support queue, that is a short list.

Drafting a first reply for a person to approve and send
Pulling order, subscription or account status into the ticket
Summarising a long thread before a human picks it up
Answering documented policy questions with a citation to the source

What to keep human

Refunds, credits, discounts and anything else that moves money out of the business. Cancellation and retention conversations. Escalated complaints. Anything touching a legal or regulatory promise. Anything where the answer is no.

That last one is the failure mode nobody expects. Anthropic's phase two writeup lists, among the remaining problems, the agent's "inability to refuse unreasonable demands" as a consequence of its helpfulness training. Models are trained to be agreeable, and your support queue contains people who will use that.
Read this before you deploy AI agents for customer support
Project Vend
, published June 2025, gave Claude a real shop, a real budget and real customers who were Anthropic employees. It ran the business autonomously. The pattern in the results is what matters.
It priced below cost.
It set prices without researching what things cost to buy.
It hallucinated a payment account.
It invented a Venmo account and told customers to send money to it. Not a wrong tone of voice. A wrong bank detail, confidently delivered.
It folded under social pressure.

Employees talked it into discount codes and giveaways over Slack, including a tungsten cube. Offered $100 for a six pack of Irn Bru available online for about $15, it said only that it would "keep the request in mind".
It raised a price exactly once
across the entire run.
It did not learn.
After acknowledging that its discount logic was losing money, it "returned to offering [discount codes] within days".

Map those onto a support queue. Confident wrong information, susceptibility to a persuasive customer, no memory of yesterday's lesson. That is the risk profile, published by the lab with the most to gain from you thinking otherwise.
What changed in phase two, and why it is the whole lesson
Phase two
, published December 2025, reached stabilized profitability across three locations. Same capability. What changed was everything around it:

Inventory tooling
with cost visibility
, so it saw what it paid before setting a price

oversight agent
checking the primary agent's decisions

The remaining failures still matter: naive compliance with an unrealistic contract, inadequate theft protection, susceptibility to social engineering, and that inability to say no. Scaffolding moved it from failing to working. It did not make it safe to leave alone.
Why a good demo tells you almost nothing
Here is the most useful number in this article, and one you will not see in a sales deck. The
tau bench paper
measures agents on realistic tool use with a simulated user. Leading function calling agents "succeed on <50% of the tasks, and are quite inconsistent", with
pass^8 under 25% in retail
pass^8 means: does the agent succeed at the same task all eight times you run it. Under a quarter of the time.

That gap between single attempt success and repeated success is the entire risk of a support deployment. A demo is one attempt. Your queue is thousands a month. An agent right 70% of the time on the first try, and inconsistent across repeats, produces a steady trickle of confidently wrong answers to customers who have no way of knowing.

How to deploy AI agents for customer support, stage by stage
Stage 0, two weeks. Instrument first.
Categorise your last 500 tickets. You need your real mix before automating any of it, and most teams find four categories cover 70% of volume.
Stage 1, two to four weeks. Classification only.
The agent reads and tags, and sends nothing. Compare its tags against your team's. If it cannot route a ticket, it cannot answer one.
Stage 2, four weeks. Drafts behind a human.
The agent writes a reply, a person presses send. Log the edit rate. If your team rewrites more than a third of drafts, your knowledge base is the problem.
Stage 3. Autonomous on one narrow category.
The most repetitive, lowest risk one from Stage 0. Order status, opening hours, a documented policy. Nothing that moves money. Keep the human path one click away.
Stage 4. Widen slowly, with a supervisor.
Add categories one at a time, plus an oversight step reviewing a sample of autonomous responses, as phase two of Project Vend did.

items.a: For common, repetitive tickets, plausibly. Gartner predicts agentic AI will [autonomously resolve 80% of **common** customer service issues by 2029](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-03-05-gartner-predicts-agentic-ai-will-autonomously-resolve-80-percent-of-common-customer-service-issues-without-human-intervention-by-20290) with a 30% cost reduction, and the word common is doing real work there. Complex, emotional and policy heavy tickets are not in that number, and should not be in your business case.

items.q: Why did my agent work in testing and fail in production?
items.a: Because single attempt success is a bad proxy for reliability. The tau bench paper found leading agents succeeding on under half of realistic tasks and scoring under 25% on pass^8, consistency across eight repeated runs. A demo tests one attempt. Production tests thousands, and the inconsistency shows up as a trickle of wrong answers.

x.s: Somebody has probably told you that you need an ITIN first. That advice is wrong, it is everywhere, and it costs founders months of waiting for a number they never needed.

Here is how to get an EIN without an SSN, in the words of the IRS rather than a formation service. The instructions for Form SS-4 say, at line 7b: "Enter 'foreign' or N/A on line 7b if the responsible party doesn't have and is ineligible to obtain an SSN or ITIN."

That single line is the whole answer. There is a designated way to write "I do not have a US tax number" on the form, and the IRS put it there on purpose, because plenty of people who need an EIN are not American.
What an EIN is and why you need one
An EIN is an Employer Identification Number, a federal tax identification number for a business entity. Despite the name, you do not need employees to have one.

You need it to open a US business bank account and to file the federal returns your company owes. Payment processors and marketplaces ask for it. If you have just formed a US LLC from abroad, it is the next thing you do after the state approves your filing.
It is not a licence and not permission to trade. It is an identifier.
You do not need an SSN or an ITIN
The confusion comes from the shape of the form. Line 7b of Form SS-4 asks for the responsible party's SSN, ITIN or EIN, and people reasonably conclude they must produce one of the three.
Read the instruction attached to that line instead. The
IRS Instructions for Form SS-4
tell you what to do when you have none of them: "Enter 'foreign' or N/A on line 7b if the responsible party doesn't have and is ineligible to obtain an SSN or ITIN."
That is not a workaround or a grey area. It is the documented procedure for your exact situation, published by the agency that issues the number.
The responsible party, for a single owner LLC, is you. It has to be a natural person who controls the entity, not another company.
Why the online application will not work for you
Everything you read points at the IRS online EIN assistant, which issues a number immediately at the end of the session. Then you start it and cannot get through.
The IRS is explicit about why. Its
EIN guidance
states that if you have no legal residence, principal place of business, or principal office or agency in the United States or US territories, you cannot use the online application to obtain an EIN.

Notice what that is and is not. It is a restriction on one web form, not a statement that you are ineligible for an EIN. The tool was built around US identity verification and cannot handle an applicant it cannot verify that way, so the IRS routes those applicants to a human instead.
One more thing about the online tool, if you do have a US address and can use it. The session expires after 15 minutes of inactivity and restarts from the beginning, so gather everything first.
The phone route for international applicants
If you are outside the US with no US presence, the fastest route is the telephone.
Call
. It is not a toll free number, so it will cost you international call rates. Lines are open 6:00 a.m. to 11:00 p.m. Eastern time, Monday to Friday.

This is a dedicated line for international applicants. An assistor takes you through Form SS-4 question by question and the number is issued on the same call. That is the entire process. No ITIN, no notarised documents, no agent.

The two practical difficulties are the time zone and the wait. Work out what 6:00 a.m. Eastern is where you are, call early in the IRS day rather than late, and expect to hold. Do not call from a phone that will run out of battery or credit halfway through.
Fax and post are the alternatives if a call is impractical. You complete Form SS-4, sign it, and send it in.

Those are the IRS's own published expectations rather than anecdotes from a forum. Real processing can run longer at busy times, but the ranking never changes: phone beats fax, fax beats post, and post is the last resort.
An EIN is free
The IRS could not put this more plainly: "Beware of websites that charge for an EIN. You never have to pay a fee for an EIN."

An entire tier of services charges to obtain a number the IRS gives away. The better ones are transparent that you are paying for admin rather than the number. The worse ones are designed to look like the IRS.

Paying somebody to make the call is a legitimate choice if the time zone is impossible or the form makes you nervous. Just be clear that you are buying an hour of somebody else's morning, not a product. The government fee is zero.
What to have in hand before you call
Get all of this on one page before you dial. The assistor works through the form in order, and hunting for a document mid call is how sessions go wrong.

What comes next
The EIN is the middle step. It sits between forming the company and the two things that actually take effort.
Next is the bank account, where the obstacle is bank policy rather than anything legal. Our guide to

After that comes the federal filing that catches almost every foreign owned LLC by surprise. If your LLC has a single owner who is not a US person,
Form 5472 and its $25,000 penalty
apply to you, and funding your own company counts as a reportable transaction. Read that one before your first year end, not after.
If you have not formed the company yet, the full sequence is in

The short version
You do not need an SSN. You do not need an ITIN. You need a formed company, a completed Form SS-4, and either a phone call at an awkward hour or a fax and some patience.

The myth persists because most content about US company formation is written by people selling formation packages, and "you need an ITIN first, we can help with that" is a better sales pitch than "write foreign on line 7b and call this number". The IRS published the instruction. It has been there the whole time.

items.q: Can I get an EIN without an SSN or ITIN?
items.a: Yes. The IRS instructions for Form SS-4 tell a responsible party who has no SSN or ITIN and cannot obtain one to enter "foreign" on line 7b. You apply by phone, fax or post rather than online, because the online tool is restricted to applicants with a US legal residence, principal place of business or principal office.

items.q: Do I need an ITIN before applying for an EIN?
items.a: No. This is the most common piece of bad advice non resident founders receive, and following it can add months to a launch for no benefit. An ITIN is an individual taxpayer number with its own separate application process. Your company's EIN does not depend on it, and line 7b of Form SS-4 tells you what to write instead.

items.q: How much does an EIN cost?
items.a: Nothing. The IRS warns directly that you never have to pay a fee for an EIN and to be careful of websites that charge for one. Third party services may charge for handling the application on your behalf, which is a service fee rather than a government fee, and you are free to make the call yourself for the price of an international phone call.

items.q: What is the IRS phone number for international EIN applications?
items.a: 267 941 1099, open 6:00 a.m. to 11:00 p.m. Eastern, Monday to Friday. It is not a toll free number. An assistor takes you through Form SS-4 on the call, and for international applicants the EIN is issued during that same call rather than posted out later.

items.q: How long does an EIN take by fax or post?
items.a: The IRS says fax applications are generally processed within 4 business days and posted applications take approximately 4 weeks. If you have any deadline at all, the phone line is the only route that gives you a number the same day.

x.s: Most people answer the question "what to automate first in a small business" by listing tools. Here is a CRM, here is a scheduler, here is a form builder, go forth. That list is useless because it tells you nothing about which of your processes is ready.

A process is ready when four things are true at once. It happens often. It needs almost no judgement. Somebody has already written it down, or could in twenty minutes. And it is currently failing in a way that a real person notices and complains about.

Miss any one and you will build something nobody uses, or something that quietly breaks and costs more than it saved. Below is the test, six candidates that usually pass it, and an honest list of what to leave alone.
The four part test
High frequency.
If it happens twice a year, automating it is a hobby. Weekly is the floor, daily is better. The value comes from repetition, not cleverness.
Low judgement.
The steps are the same every time, or vary in ways you can write as a rule. "Send the welcome pack" qualifies. "Decide whether this client is a good fit" does not.
Already written down.
Not in someone's head. Written. If you cannot describe the process in numbered steps, you do not have a process, you have a habit, and automating a habit produces chaos at speed. Our
SOP examples for a small service business
post has templates for this.
Visibly failing.

Something drops. Invoices go out late, leads sit unanswered overnight, onboarding emails get missed. If nobody notices the current version failing, nobody will notice the automated version working either.
What small businesses actually use AI for, according to the Census

Before picking a candidate, know how shallow real adoption is. The marketing makes it sound like everyone is running fleets of agents. They are not. Census Bureau research published in April 2026 found that
about 57% of adopters use AI in three or fewer business functions
. Not three or fewer departments transformed. Three or fewer functions touched at all.

Two more numbers from the same paper are worth holding onto. Only

report AI related employment decreases, and

use AI to augment work rather than replace it. That is the realistic picture. Nobody is firing their operations person. They are getting enquiries answered faster.
A worker level survey looks like it disagrees. The US Chamber of Commerce Foundation and Ipsos found that
50% of small business workers use AI at work

, from a probability sample of 1,070 employed adults fielded in May 2026. Both are true. The Census asks a company officer whether the business used AI in producing goods or services. The Chamber asks workers about any use at all. Most small business AI is one employee quietly using a chatbot, which is why only
of those workers said they use it for workflow automation. That 6% is roughly the size of the real opportunity.

x.s: Take them in order of how loudly they are failing, not the order listed.
Inbound enquiry routing

is the one I would pick first for most service businesses. The trigger is unambiguous, the steps never change, and the failure is visible the moment a lead sits for a day. It also sits in Sales and Marketing, where the Census data says adoption happens.
New client onboarding
is the highest value one, and the hardest, because it touches the most systems. Do it second, after you have proved the pattern works.
Meeting notes to actions
is where an AI model genuinely earns its keep early, because summarising and extracting structured data from text is what these models are reliably good at.
Weekly reporting
is the least glamorous and often the best return, because it replaces a recurring job that a human hates and does badly.
Build the simplest thing that works

The strongest advice on this comes from Anthropic's own engineering team, who build these systems and have no incentive to talk you out of buying more of them. Their guidance is to find "the simplest solution possible, and only increasing complexity when needed", and they warn that "the autonomous nature of agents means higher costs, and the potential for compounding errors".
They also draw a line worth memorising. Workflows are
systems where LLMs and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths
. Agents are systems where the model directs its own process.

Almost everything on the candidate list above is a workflow. A form arrives, five things happen in a fixed order. There is no decision for a model to make, so putting one in the middle adds cost, latency and a new way to fail. Reach for an agent when the flexibility is the point, not because agents are what the industry is selling. The cost side of that choice is broken down in our post on
how much AI automation costs
What not to automate first
Anything that needs to be right nearly every time.
The tau bench benchmark measures whether an agent completes the same task correctly on all eight attempts, and found that leading function calling agents scored
under 25% on that measure in retail scenarios

, while succeeding on fewer than half of single attempts. Something that works when you demo it can still fail one run in three. If a wrong output means a wrong invoice, a wrong payment or a lost customer, that process is not first.
Anything customer facing you have not watched run.
Build it, then run it in shadow mode, where the output goes to you instead of the customer, for a couple of weeks. You will find things.
Anything not yet written down.
Automation encodes a process. If the process only exists as folklore, you will encode three different people's versions of it and discover the conflict in production.
Anything you are about to change.
If you are switching CRM next quarter, wait.
What to do this month
Pick one process. Write it down in numbered steps, with a trigger at the top and a definition of done at the bottom. Count how many times it ran last month.
Then build the smallest possible version. Not the one with branching logic for every edge case. The one that handles the eighty percent case and pings a human on anything else.
Watch it for four weeks. Count what it caught and what it missed. Only then decide whether a second one is worth doing. If you want a structured way to pick the right first process, our
automation assessment
walks through it.
The short version

Automation is a selection decision more than a technology decision. Pick the wrong process and the best tooling produces something nobody trusts. Pick the right one and a dull sequence of connected apps quietly removes a recurring annoyance from your week.
The test is worth repeating because it is all of it. High frequency, low judgement, already written down, visibly failing. If a process fails any of those, it is not first. It might be third.

items.q: What should a small business automate first?
items.a: The process that runs at least weekly, needs no judgement, is already written down in steps, and is currently failing in a way somebody complains about. For most service businesses that is inbound enquiry routing, because the trigger is clear and a slow response is immediately visible. Onboarding is more valuable but touches more systems, so it works better second.

items.q: Do I need AI to automate a small business process?
items.a: Usually not for the first one. Most small business processes are fixed sequences, and a deterministic workflow that runs the same way every time is cheaper and easier to debug than a model deciding what to do. Anthropic's own guidance is to use the simplest solution that works. Add a model where you need text summarised, classified or extracted.

items.q: How many processes should I automate at once?
items.a: One. Census data shows most firms that adopt AI touch three or fewer business functions, and those are the ones getting value. Building four automations in a month means debugging four things simultaneously with no baseline to compare against. Ship one, watch it for a month, then decide.

items.q: Is automation going to replace my staff?
items.a: The Census data says almost never. Only 2% of firms report AI related employment decreases, and 66% of adopters use it to augment work rather than replace it. In a small business the realistic outcome is that the person who was chasing invoices manually now spends that hour on work that needs a human.

items.q: What is the most common reason a first automation fails?
items.a: The process was not written down properly, so the automation encodes assumptions nobody agreed to. The second most common reason is choosing something customer facing before watching it run in private. Both are avoidable with a fortnight of patience.

x.s: Most penalties in the US tax system scale with what you owe. This one does not. The Form 5472 foreign owned LLC penalty is a flat $25,000, and it applies to a company that made no money, has no customers and owes no tax.

That is the part people cannot believe. You can form a US LLC, move a few hundred dollars into its account to cover the registered agent, never trade, and still have a federal filing obligation with a five figure penalty attached to missing it.
The IRS wording is not open to interpretation: "A penalty of $25,000 will be assessed on any reporting corporation that fails to file Form 5472 when due and in the manner prescribed."
Below is who files, why a dormant company usually still has to, what you send and where, and how the penalty works.
Who has to file
The rule targets a specific and very common structure: a US limited liability company with one owner, where that owner is not a US person.

For most purposes the IRS ignores that kind of company. It is a disregarded entity, meaning its income is treated as the owner's. For this one purpose the treatment flips: a foreign owned US disregarded entity counts as a corporation under the reporting rules. That is why a company with one foreign member ends up filing a corporate form.
You are in scope if all of these are true:

items.s: The entity is a US business entity, typically an LLC
It has one owner for tax purposes
That owner is a foreign person, a non US individual or a foreign entity
The company had at least one reportable transaction in the tax year

x.s: That last condition is where almost everyone goes wrong.
Why a dormant LLC usually still has to file
Founders read "reportable transaction" and picture invoices, sales, contracts. Something commercial. Then they conclude a company with no revenue has nothing to report.
The
IRS Instructions for Form 5472

define it much more broadly. For a foreign owned US disregarded entity, reportable transactions include "amounts paid or received in connection with the formation, dissolution, acquisition, and disposition of the entity, including contributions to, and distributions from, the entity."
Read that again with your own bank account in mind.

Money you put in is a contribution. Money you take out is a distribution. Paying the formation fee from your personal card is an amount paid in connection with the formation of the entity. Each is a reportable transaction between you and your company.

So the practical position is this: if you funded the company at all, in any amount, you have a filing obligation. An LLC that never received a cent and never spent one may fall outside the requirement, but that company is rarer than people assume.
Treat "we had no revenue so there is nothing to file" as the assumption that creates the penalty.
What you actually file
This is the second surprise. You do not file Form 5472 on its own.
You file a
pro forma Form 1120

, the US corporation income tax return, with Form 5472 attached. Pro forma here means you are not filing a real corporate return and not reporting corporate income. You are using the 1120 as an envelope.
The instructions are specific about how to mark it. Write
"Foreign-owned U.S. DE"
across the top of page 1 of the Form 1120. That exact phrase, in that place, is what tells the IRS what the filing is and stops it being processed as an ordinary corporate return.

On that pro forma 1120 you complete only the entity's name and address and items B and E. The rest is left alone. The substance is in the attached Form 5472, which asks about the foreign owner, the related parties, and the amounts involved in the reportable transactions.
The deadline is the Form 1120 due date for the tax year, including extensions.
Where to send it
These filings do not go to the ordinary corporate return address. The wrong one lands you in the "failed to file in the manner prescribed" category.

Keep proof of what you sent and when. If you fax, keep the confirmation. If you post, use a service that evidences delivery. The penalty here is severe enough that proving you filed is worth a few extra dollars.
The penalty, precisely
The headline number gets attention, but the continuation penalty turns an oversight into a serious problem.

The IRS instructions state that a penalty of $25,000 will be assessed on any reporting corporation that fails to file Form 5472 when due and in the manner prescribed. The same penalty applies to failing to maintain the records the form requires.

Then the continuation piece. If the failure continues more than 90 days after the IRS notifies you, an additional $25,000 applies for each 30 day period, or fraction of a 30 day period, that it continues after that window.

rows.s: Failure to file when due, or not in the manner prescribed
Each 30 day period, or part of one, beyond 90 days after IRS notification

x.s: Source:
IRS Instructions for Form 5472
Note the phrase "or fraction of". A single day into a new 30 day period counts as that whole period, and the arithmetic compounds quickly.

Note also "in the manner prescribed". Filing something is not automatically filing correctly. A 5472 sent without the pro forma 1120, without the required marking, or to the wrong address is exactly what that language covers.
What to do about it
Put the deadline in a calendar the day you form the company, not the day you remember it exists. This form has an annual rhythm and no reminder letter.

Keep a record of every movement of money between you and the company, in both directions, with dates and amounts. That record is the raw material for the form and it is what the records penalty refers to. A spreadsheet is enough. Doing it as you go takes minutes; reconstructing it eleven months later takes a weekend.

Then get a US tax preparer. This is general information, not tax advice, and I am not going to pretend otherwise. Anyone with a foreign owned single member LLC should use a preparer who has handled this filing before. Professional help is cheap next to a $25,000 mistake, and the rules interact with your own country's tax position in ways no article can assess.

If you have already missed a year, that is a conversation to have with a preparer promptly rather than a reason to keep quiet. The continuation penalty runs from IRS notification, so time is not neutral.
The uncomfortable summary

Nothing about this filing is intuitive. It is a corporate return you do not really file, attached to an information return you have never heard of, marked with a phrase you write by hand, posted to an address that appears on no other IRS form, for a company that may have made no money. That is why people miss it.

The formation services that sold you the LLC in twenty minutes mostly do not mention it, because it happens a year later and it is not their problem. The penalty is real and it does not care that the company was dormant.

items.q: Does a foreign owned LLC with no income have to file Form 5472?
items.a: Usually yes. The trigger is a reportable transaction, not revenue, and the IRS definition includes contributions to and distributions from the entity. Funding your own LLC's bank account or paying its formation costs is a reportable transaction, so a company with no sales normally still has a filing obligation for that year.

items.q: What is the penalty for not filing Form 5472?
items.a: $25,000 for failing to file when due and in the manner prescribed, per the IRS instructions. If the failure continues more than 90 days after IRS notification, a further $25,000 applies for each 30 day period or fraction of one after that. The same penalty applies to failing to maintain the required records.

items.q: Do I file Form 5472 by itself?
items.a: No. You attach it to a pro forma Form 1120 and write "Foreign-owned U.S. DE" across the top of page 1. Only the name and address and items B and E of the 1120 need completing. The package goes to the dedicated Ogden address or fax number rather than the normal corporate return address.

items.q: When is Form 5472 due for a foreign owned LLC?
items.a: It is due with the pro forma Form 1120, on the Form 1120 due date for the tax year, including any extensions you properly obtained. Because it rides on a corporate deadline rather than an individual one, the date catches out founders used to personal tax timelines at home.

items.q: Does this apply if my LLC has two owners?
items.a: The rules here apply to a foreign owned US disregarded entity, meaning a single owner LLC. A multiple owner LLC is normally taxed as a partnership and has different obligations, which may include reporting on foreign partners. Different form, same principle: check before the year ends rather than after.

The Agency Wallet, and why bills arrive unannounced
Usage is not invoiced monthly alongside the subscription. It is funded from an

Two practical consequences. First, your usage spending is separate from your subscription, so looking at your card statement for the $97 tells you almost nothing about what the platform actually costs you. Second, if the wallet runs dry, the things funded by it stop, which for most setups means messaging stops.
If you are on Unlimited or Agency Pro and rebilling clients, the wallet is also the mechanism that funds their usage before you recover it. So it needs a real balance and someone watching it.

I want to be exact, because this gets glossed over constantly. The rates are not buried on a subpage. There is no published rate card for GoHighLevel telephony at all. The cost depends on Twilio's rates for your country, your number type, your message segment count and your carrier fees, all set outside HighLevel.

anyone who quotes you a total monthly GoHighLevel cost that includes text messaging is guessing.
They may be guessing from experience, and a good estimate from someone who runs similar accounts is worth having. But it is an estimate, and you should be told that it is one.

If texting is central to your business, and for most service businesses chasing leads it is, treat telephony as an unknown, run a month at low volume, measure your actual wallet drawdown, and only then build a budget.

How many sub accounts.
One is a build. Twelve is a system with a template, and the second one onward is far cheaper than the first.

Two service lines sharing a process is one build. Two with different stages, owners and follow up rules is two.

The big one, and it is the same on every platform. A build from a documented process is a known job. A build from a conversation is priced as risk, which is why quotes for the same request vary so widely.

A clean export with sensible fields is straightforward. Fifteen years of a legacy system with free text everywhere is a different project.

Adding your whole team costs nothing. What costs extra is what you send and how many premium automation steps run.

items.q: How much does GoHighLevel charge for SMS?
items.a: HighLevel does not publish SMS, MMS, voice or phone number rates. They are Twilio pass through, priced by country, number type, message segments and carrier fees. Anyone quoting a total monthly cost that includes texting is estimating. Run a low volume month, measure your wallet drawdown, then budget from your own data.

items.q: Do I need the $297 plan?
items.a: Only if you need more than 3 sub accounts or you want to rebill usage to clients at cost. Rebilling with a markup requires the $497 Agency Pro plan. A single business with one brand and no client billing can run on Starter at $97 a month indefinitely.

items.q: What does a GoHighLevel setup cost to build?
items.a: There is no published market rate, so treat any confident average as unsourced. The price is driven by the number of sub accounts and pipelines, how much data is migrating, how much automation you need, and above all whether your process is documented before anyone starts.

items.q: Is there a free version of GoHighLevel?
items.a: No. There is a 14 day free trial and then the lowest paid plan is $97 a month. Unlike HubSpot, which has a genuinely permanent free tier for up to 2 users, GoHighLevel has no free plan.

x.s: Most comparisons of these two argue about features. Wrong argument. For a plumbing company, a clinic, a law firm or an agency with six people, both platforms will do the job.
What does not converge is the billing. GoHighLevel vs HubSpot for a small service business comes down to one fact: these two companies charge you for opposite things.

HubSpot charges per seat and per marketing contact, so it gets more expensive as your team and your list grow. GoHighLevel charges a flat platform fee with unlimited users and unlimited contacts and meters what you send, so it gets more expensive as your message volume grows.
Pick the one whose cost curve points away from the direction you are growing in. That is the whole decision, and below is the arithmetic.

A worked comparison for a real small service business
Take a business that exists everywhere. Six people, four of whom work in the CRM daily. A contact list of 4,000. About 12,000 marketing and follow up emails a month, with automation behind it.
On HubSpot

Marketing Hub Starter is $7 per seat a month on annual billing and includes 1,000 marketing contacts. Four seats is $28 a month. Then the list. Importing 4,000 contacts adds roughly $150 a month in contact overage, because additional contacts at Starter are priced at $50 per 1,000 from 1,001 to 3,000, then $45 per 1,000, then $40. That schedule is published in
HubSpot's product and services catalog
Add Sales Hub Starter for the same four people at $7 per seat and you are at another $28.
Running total: about $206 a month, roughly $2,472 a year.
No onboarding fee at Starter.
On GoHighLevel
Starter is $97 a month, or $970 a year, with unlimited users, unlimited contacts and a cap of 3 sub accounts. All six people get logins. All 4,000 contacts sit there. Neither costs extra.
Then the metering:

On a single month those two numbers decide nothing. What decides it is what happens next.
The part that actually decides it: which direction are you growing
Change one variable at a time and watch what each platform does.
You hire two more people.
HubSpot goes up by $14 a month per person across both hubs, so roughly $28 more a month. GoHighLevel does not move at all.
Your list doubles to 8,000.
HubSpot's contact overage climbs into the next bands. GoHighLevel still does not move.
You triple your email and automation volume.
HubSpot barely notices, because you are paying for contacts, not sends. GoHighLevel goes from about $88 a month in metered usage to about $264.
You start texting every lead within five minutes.
HubSpot's price does not change. GoHighLevel's does, by an amount neither of us can calculate. That is the next section.

So a big team with a big list that communicates modestly is cheaper on GoHighLevel. A small team with a small list that sends constantly is cheaper on HubSpot. Most service businesses I speak to are the first kind and assume they are the second.
The honest gap in the GoHighLevel numbers

GoHighLevel publishes its email rate, its validation rate and its workflow execution rate. It does not publish its telephony rates. Phone numbers, SMS, MMS and voice are billed as Twilio pass through, and HighLevel does not publish a rate card for them.

That is a real limitation on any comparison, including this one. If somebody hands you a complete monthly GoHighLevel figure that includes texting, they estimated it. Possibly well, but you should know that is what happened. Full metered layer in
how much a GoHighLevel setup actually costs

The equivalent uncertainty on the HubSpot side is smaller but real: HubSpot does not list a monthly price for Sales Hub Enterprise, and an extra Marketing Hub core seat shows as $45 a month on the pricing page and $50 in the legal catalog. On ten extra seats that gap is $600 a year.
Being fair to HubSpot
Two things HubSpot does that nobody else here does.
The free tier is genuinely permanent and genuinely usable.
Not a trial. Up to 2 users, no expiry. A solo operator or a two person shop can run a real pipeline on it indefinitely.
View only seats are free and unlimited on paid portals.

Your bookkeeper, operations manager and assistant can all see what is happening without adding a cent. HubSpot also removed seat minimums effective 5 March 2024, killing the old trap where a two person business had to buy five.
HubSpot's own announcement

The counterweight is the lock in. HubSpot's terms state that "You are not permitted to downgrade your Subscription Service during your Current Term", and on seats that "the total count can't be reduced until your next renewal date". Contact tiers work the same way.
Being fair to GoHighLevel

GoHighLevel was designed for agencies, and it shows even if you are not one. The sub account structure lets one platform hold several distinct businesses or locations. Starter caps you at 3 sub accounts. Unlimited at $297 a month removes the cap.
Rebilling is where the agency design becomes a cost decision.
Rebilling usage at cost requires the $297 Unlimited plan. Rebilling with a markup requires the $497 Agency Pro plan.
If you plan to pass texting costs on to clients, you are not on the $97 plan, whatever the comparison table said.

There is also a real add on layer: AI Employee at $50 a month per location on Growth and $97 on Unlimited, HIPAA compliance at $297 a month, a white label mobile app at $497 a month, and others between $10 and $500 a month. Usage is funded through an Agency Wallet you top up. There is a 14 day free trial and no permanent free tier.

I would not choose between these two on features. I would choose on which number in your business is going up fastest over the next two years.

If that number is people or contacts, GoHighLevel's flat fee is a genuine structural advantage and it does not degrade as you grow. If that number is messages, HubSpot's per contact model is the safer bill, and you get a permanent free tier to prove the process works before you pay anything.

x.s: In July 2026, Americans filed
578,926 business applications
, up 8.1% on June. That gets reported as "578,926 new businesses", which is not what it is, and the difference matters.

A business application in the Census data is an application for an Employer Identification Number. It is a form, not a registered company and not a trading business, and a large share of them never become either. Census separates out high propensity applications, the ones likely to become employer businesses. In July 2026 that was 151,857, roughly 26% of the total.
So here is how to set up a business in 2026 in the order the steps unblock each other, with the real fee or deadline attached to each.
The failure statistic you have been told
You have read that 90% of startups fail. It is everywhere, and it has no basis in any BLS or Census dataset I can find. Here is what the Bureau of Labor Statistics actually publishes:
Source:
BLS Business Employment Dynamics, Table 7

Read across the 2015 row. About one in five establishments do not survive year one, roughly 45% are gone within five years, and about 37% are there at ten. So the defensible number is that around 63% fail within a decade. Bad, but very different from 90%, and BLS notes that
survival rates follow a similar path regardless of birth year
, so this is stable rather than a pandemic artefact.
Why start here. Because 90% makes setup feel like a lottery ticket, and the real numbers make it what it is, a thing where most survivors did the boring parts.
How to set up a business in 2026, in dependency order
Seven stages, each there because the next will not work without it.

x.s: Most guides put the website first because a website is fun and paperwork is not. That costs weeks, because you cannot take a payment into an account you do not have, cannot open the account without the EIN, and cannot get the EIN without the entity.
Stage 1: decide the structure
Three realistic options, and the choice is mostly about who will own it.
LLC.
Cheapest, simplest, flexible. The default for most small businesses.
C Corp.
Federal rate is a
flat 21%

, and the SBA is blunt about the cost: "Corporate profits are taxed twice, first, when the company makes a profit, and again when dividends are paid to shareholders." The return is due on the 15th day of the 4th month after year end. Choose this when raising outside investment.
S Corp.
An election, made on Form 2553, not a separate entity type. The
restrictions
are strict: a domestic corporation, no more than 100 shareholders, one class of stock, and shareholders limited to individuals and certain trusts and estates.

Those rules are why an S Corp cannot take venture money. VC funds are usually partnerships or LLCs, so they are not eligible shareholders. Foreign investors are not eligible either, and preferred stock is a second class of stock. Any one of the three ends the conversation.
If you might ever sell, Qualified Small Business Stock relief under

applies to domestic C corporation stock and explicitly not to S corporation stock. For stock issued after 4 July 2025 the gross assets limit rose to $75,000,000 and the holding period became tiered, at 50% relief after three years and 100% after five.
Stage 2: form the entity

Filing fees range from $50 in New Mexico and Colorado to $425 in Nevada, and the annual cost from nothing in Ohio to $800 a year in California. Delaware's annual LLC tax rose to $400 in 2026, which most comparison articles have not caught up with.
The full ten state table is in our guide to
choosing between Wyoming, Delaware and New Mexico
, with the honest answer about forming out of state, which is that for a business with a physical home it usually costs more.
A registered agent is mandatory everywhere. Physical street address in the state, someone there during business hours to accept legal service. A PO box will not do.
Stage 3: get the EIN
The EIN is free. The IRS says so plainly: "Beware of websites that charge for an EIN. You never have to pay a fee for an EIN."
Timelines, from the
IRS instructions

rows.s: Immediate, issued at the end of the session

x.s: Two traps. The online session times out after 15 minutes of inactivity and restarts from the beginning. And if you have no legal residence, principal place of business or principal office in the United States, the tool is closed to you.

The bigger myth is that you need a Social Security Number. You do not. The IRS instructions say to enter "foreign" or N/A on line 7b where the responsible party has no SSN or ITIN and cannot get one. International applicants call 267 941 1099, not toll free, open 6:00 a.m. to 11:00 p.m. Eastern. Full process in
getting an EIN without an SSN
Stage 4: open the bank account
If you are a US person this is ordinary. If not, you have probably been told you need an SSN. You do not.
Under FinCEN's Customer Identification Program rule,

, a bank may accept from a non US person a taxpayer identification number, a passport number and country of issuance, an alien identification card number, or another government issued document evidencing nationality or residence and bearing a photograph. A passport is legally sufficient. What stops people is bank policy, covered in
opening a US bank account as a non resident
Good news for 2026. FinCEN's final rule of 11 August 2026
permanently removes the requirement for US companies and US persons to report beneficial ownership information
under the Corporate Transparency Act. Almost every setup guide still tells you to file a BOI report. One nuance: a foreign company registering in a US state is still a reporting company.
Stage 5: the money side
Invoicing, payments, and the filings that follow money.

If your LLC has a single owner who is not a US person, the expensive one lives here. Form 5472 applies to a foreign owned US disregarded entity with any reportable transaction in the tax year, and that includes amounts paid or received in connection with the formation of the entity, including contributions to it. Funding your own LLC's account counts. The
IRS instructions

state that a penalty of $25,000 will be assessed on any reporting corporation that fails to file when due, with a further $25,000 for each 30 day period beyond 90 days after notification. Walkthrough in our
Form 5472 guide
Stage 6: the customer side
Now, and only now, the website and CRM.
A site that cannot get an enquiry into somewhere you will actually look is a brochure. Get the capture working before the hero image. Our notes on
choosing a CRM
go through the tools without pretending one wins, and
website development
and
CRM and sales systems
are the service versions.
Stage 7: the operating layer
Write down how the work gets done before you hire anyone to do it.
The least glamorous stage, and the one deciding whether the business can exist without you. Start with the three processes you repeat most. Examples in our post on
SOPs for small businesses
, and
operations and HR
is the service version.

The legal minimum to exist as a company is often under $200. Everything above that is a choice about how fast you move.
Where people actually get stuck
Not on the filing. That is a form and a fee.

They get stuck between stage 4 and stage 5, holding a company that legally exists and cannot take money, and between stage 6 and stage 7, running a business that works only when they personally do everything. Both are ordinary problems with ordinary fixes.
Pick the stage you are stuck at and finish that one.

items.q: How long does it take to set up a business in 2026?
items.a: The entity takes days, depending on the state and whether you expedite. The EIN is immediate online, four business days by fax, or roughly four weeks by mail. Banking is the variable step, from an afternoon to several weeks.

items.q: Is the 90% startup failure rate real?
items.a: No. It has no BLS or Census basis. The published survival data shows about 78% of new establishments surviving their first year and about 37% surviving to ten, so roughly 63% fail within a decade. Still hard, but a different claim, and nobody sourced the 90%.

items.q: Are business applications the same as new businesses?
items.a: No, and this is the most common error in the topic. Census business applications are EIN applications, and many never become operating companies. The separate high propensity figure was 151,857 of the 578,926 filed in July 2026.

items.q: Do I still need to file a BOI report?
items.a: Not if you are a US company or a US person. FinCEN's final rule of 11 August 2026 permanently removed the requirement and is deleting information previously reported by US persons. A foreign company registering in a US state is still a reporting company.
