x.s: Every comparison of n8n vs Make vs Zapier for a small business opens with a feature grid. Connectors, branching, error handling, who has the nicer editor. Those grids are interchangeable now and none will tell you which tool to pick.

What decides it is how each platform counts your usage. Zapier charges per successful action. Make charges per credit, which is roughly per action. n8n charges per execution, meaning one whole run of your workflow no matter how many steps are inside it.

Those are different units, and the same automation can cost eight times more on one than another purely because of the unit. Below are the definitions in each vendor's own words, a worked example, the plan tables as of September 2026, and a straight answer at the end.
How each platform counts, in its own words
Zapier
is explicit in its help documentation:
"A task is any successful action that runs in Zapier. Only successful actions count toward your task usage."
Make
puts it this way on its pricing page:
"Each action your scenario performs consumes a certain number of credits, most actions consume 1 credit, while some advanced features leveraging Make's AI Provider may use more."
n8n
describes something structurally different:
"An execution is a single run of your entire workflow. It doesn't matter how many steps are in the workflow or how much data it processes. It's still a single execution."
Read those again. Two price the inside of your workflow. One prices the outside.
The worked example that settles it

Take an ordinary automation. A form comes in, the lead is checked against your CRM, created if new, tagged, assigned to an owner, a Slack alert fires, a confirmation email sends, and a row lands in a reporting sheet. That is eight actions, and say it runs 2,000 times a month.
Sources:
Zapier task definition
Make pricing
n8n pricing
. Checked September 2026.
Sixteen thousand tasks puts you well up Zapier's tier ladder. Two thousand executions sits inside n8n's €20 entry plan, and costs nothing in licence fees if you host it yourself.

Now flip it. Forty tiny two action automations firing fifty times a month come to 4,000 tasks on Zapier and 2,000 executions on n8n, and the gap almost disappears. Shape matters more than volume, so count the steps in your real processes before you believe anyone's recommendation, including mine. More on that in our post on
how much AI automation costs
What Zapier does not count, which most comparisons get wrong
This matters because it softens the per action model considerably. Zapier does not charge a task for:

items.s: Any trigger step, including polling
Filters, formatters, paths, delays and looping steps
Sub Zap, Digest, Manager and Storage steps

x.s: It does charge for action steps, steps inside error handler paths, steps that run during a replay, and Sub Zap actions.
Zapier's help centre lists all of this

A Zap that watches a form, filters out anything without a phone number, reformats a date, splits down two paths and then performs three actions is not an eight task run. It is a three task run. Tables that count every box overstate Zapier's cost, sometimes by half. What bites is a workflow of genuine actions, one write after another across five systems.
Make now bills in credits, not operations

If you are reading a Make comparison written before this year, its units are wrong. Make used to describe usage in "operations", and most comparison articles online still do. Its current pricing page describes credits. Most actions consume one, but Make's own wording is that "some advanced features leveraging Make's AI Provider may use more".

Error handlers and routers consume zero credits, which helps. A module that processes fifty bundles runs fifty times, which does not. So budget Make with a margin on top of your action count, not at parity.

Self hosting n8n: free is not the same as free
The Community Edition of n8n has no licence fee under n8n's Sustainable Use License. You pay for the server and nothing else, and for long workflows at volume it is by far the cheapest option here.

Now the honest part. Self hosting means you own the uptime. If the container falls over at 2am on the night your busiest workflow runs, nobody gets paged except you. You own the upgrades, the backups, the secrets and the security patching, and an automation platform holds API keys to your CRM, your email and probably your payments.
That is a real job, not a checkbox. If somebody in the business enjoys running infrastructure, self hosted n8n is excellent value. If nobody does, the €20 cloud plan is cheaper than the first outage.
n8n vs Make vs Zapier: which to pick
Pick Zapier if

the people building automations are not technical, your workflows are short, and you value the largest connector library. The per action model is fine when your actions are few and your filters and formatters are free.
Pick Make if
you want visual branching and heavy data transformation at a lower entry price than Zapier. Watch credit consumption if you add AI steps.
Pick n8n if

your workflows are long, you run them often, or you want the option of self hosting later. Per execution billing is the biggest structural cost advantage available to a small business running multi step automations, and unlimited steps means you never redesign a workflow to save money.
Pick none of them yet if
you have not written the process down. These tools encode a process, and if it only lives in someone's head you will pay a platform to run your confusion faster. Start with the
SOP templates
The short version

There is no winner here, which is annoying but true. There is a unit of measurement, and the right tool is the one whose unit matches the shape of what you build. Long workflows favour n8n overwhelmingly. Short ones make the difference small enough that ease of use should decide it.

Whatever you pick, do the arithmetic first. Steps times monthly runs, against the vendor's unit. It beats any comparison article, this one included, because only you know how many steps your processes have. Our guide to

covers the question that comes before this one.

items.q: Is n8n really cheaper than Zapier?
items.a: For long workflows, yes, and by a wide margin. An eight step workflow running 2,000 times a month is 16,000 Zapier tasks against 2,000 n8n executions, because n8n charges per whole run. For lots of very short workflows the difference shrinks. Count your steps and monthly runs first, because the answer depends on the shape of your automations.

items.q: Does Zapier charge for triggers and filters?
items.a: No. Zapier's help documentation confirms that trigger steps, polling, filters, formatters, paths, delays and looping steps do not count toward task usage. Only successful actions do. This is the most commonly misreported thing about Zapier pricing, and it means real bills are often lower than comparison tables predict.

items.q: What changed about Make's pricing?
items.a: Make now meters in credits rather than the "operations" that older comparison articles describe. Most actions still consume one credit, but Make states that features using its AI Provider may consume more. Any comparison written before this change uses the wrong unit, so check the date on what you read.

items.q: Is self hosted n8n free?
items.a: There is no licence fee for the Community Edition under n8n's Sustainable Use License, so the software costs nothing. You still pay for the server, and you take on uptime, upgrades, backups and security. Budget the time, not just the hosting bill. If nobody wants that job, the cloud Starter plan is cheaper in practice.

items.q: Which one should a business with two people pick?
items.a: Usually Zapier or Make, because the constraint at that size is time, not money. Move to n8n when your workflows get long enough that per action billing hurts, or when you want to self host. n8n also offers 50% off its Business plan for companies under 20 employees, which changes the maths at the top end.

The current digital incorporation fee published by Companies House is

One thing before we go further. Most people reading Calpir are American, and a UK limited company is not the default answer for you. This is for the case where you are weighing one deliberately: a UK based cofounder, UK customers who want to buy from a UK entity, a platform that requires one. If none of that describes you, our

A note on how I am presenting these. GOV.UK does not state a commencement date for the current figures on that page, so I am publishing them as the fees in force as of September 2026 rather than claiming a date on which they changed. If the exact effective date matters, for a filing you made earlier this year say, ask Companies House directly rather than trusting any blog, including this one.

The confirmation statement line catches people out for a second reason. It is £50 for the first one in a 12 month period, so filing an updated statement again inside that window does not cost another £50. An annual charge in practice, not a per filing one.
How to set up a UK limited company, step by step
The sequence is short, and the parts that go wrong are almost never the parts people worry about.
Choose the name and check it is available.
Names are checked against the Companies House register at the point of application.
Decide the registered office address.
The step with new rules, covered in its own section below because it is now the most common reason an application creates problems later.
Provide a registered email address.
Also new, also below.
File the incorporation.
Digitally at £100, on paper at £124, or via approved software at £156 for a same day service.
Tell HMRC when the company becomes active.
There is a hard deadline on this one and almost nobody mentions it. Details further down.
How long it takes
Online registration is usually completed within 24 hours. Postal registration takes 8 to 10 days, according to
GOV.UK's own guidance

So the paper route costs £24 more and roughly a week and a half. There is no scenario where posting is better unless you cannot file online at all. Same day incorporation exists at £156, but only through filing software rather than the standard web service, which in practice means going through an agent.
The registered office rules changed, and this is where people get caught
The registered office is not a formality any more. Current
GOV.UK guidance
sets out several requirements that did not all exist a few years ago.
It must be a physical UK address
, in the same part of the UK the company is registered in. A company registered in England and Wales needs an address in England or Wales.
It must be an appropriate address.

That means an address where post sent to the company would be expected to come to the attention of someone acting for it, and where delivery can be acknowledged. The test is whether mail actually reaches you and can be confirmed.
Royal Mail PO Boxes are no longer permitted.
This is the change that catches the most people, because using a PO Box was normal and widely recommended. It is not allowed now.
A registered email address is required
, and it is not published on the public register. Worth saying clearly, because people assume providing an email means exposing it.
Failure to maintain a valid registered office address can lead to strike off.
That is the company being removed from the register. Not a fine, the end of the company.

So if you were planning to use a mail forwarding service, check that what you are buying meets the appropriate address test and is not a Royal Mail PO Box wearing a nicer name. And if you use a home address, understand that the registered office is public.
The three month rule that costs people money
Once your company is active, you have a deadline that is measured from when you start trading, not from when you incorporated.
GOV.UK is explicit: "You must tell HMRC within 3 months of starting your tax accounting period if your limited company is within the charge of Corporation Tax and is now active."
Source

Three months. From starting the accounting period, not from registration, and the two are often different dates because plenty of companies incorporate and then sit dormant for a while before doing any business. Registering the company at Companies House does not do this for you. It is a separate notification to a separate agency.
This is the single most skipped step in every UK formation guide I have read, and it is the one with a clock on it.
Should an American founder set up a UK limited company at all
Probably not, if you are asking generally. Here is the honest comparison on the numbers alone.

Costs are broadly comparable and neither side wins decisively, which means cost is not the deciding factor. Anyone telling you a UK company is cheaper, or a US LLC is, is comparing two numbers out of a much longer list.

The reasons that justify a UK entity are structural rather than financial. A UK based cofounder or employees. Customers who are UK businesses and prefer to contract with a UK supplier. A platform or payment provider that requires one. Genuinely operating in the UK rather than incorporating there for optics.

The reason that does not justify it is thinking it will simplify your tax position. Running entities in two countries is a tax question with real consequences in both, one for an accountant qualified in both, not for a blog. I run Calpir from a company registered in Bristol, so I have opinions, and none of them are advice about your situation.

The short version

Budget £100 rather than £50, file online rather than by post, and treat the registered office requirement as a real decision rather than a box. Then put a reminder in your calendar for the HMRC notification, because that is the deadline with teeth and the one that no formation service handles on your behalf.
If you are American and reading this to work out whether a UK company is worth it, the fees are not the reason to do it or not do it. The reason is whether you genuinely operate there.

items.a: £100 to incorporate digitally, £124 on paper, or £156 for a same day service filed through approved software. The confirmation statement afterwards is £50 for the first one in any 12 month period. Those are the current Companies House published figures as of September 2026, not the £50 and £34 that older guides quote.

items.q: Why do so many sites still say £50?
items.a: Because £50 was the digital incorporation fee set in May 2024, and most formation content was written once and never revisited. Fee pages are boring to maintain and the number changed quietly. Check the GOV.UK fees page directly, which is the primary source and is dated on the page itself.

items.q: How long does it take to register a UK company?
items.a: Online registration is usually completed within 24 hours. Postal applications take 8 to 10 days. There is also a same day option at £156, available only through filing software rather than the standard online service, so you will usually go through an agent to use it.

items.q: Can I use a PO Box as my registered office?
items.a: No. Royal Mail PO Boxes are no longer permitted. The registered office must be an appropriate address, meaning post sent there would be expected to reach someone acting for the company and delivery can be acknowledged. Failing to maintain a valid address can lead to the company being struck off.

items.q: Do I have to tell HMRC separately after registering?
items.a: Yes. Registering at Companies House does not notify HMRC that the company is trading. You must tell HMRC within three months of starting your tax accounting period that the company is within the charge of Corporation Tax and is now active. Three months from starting the period, which is often not the incorporation date.

items.a: No. A registered email address is now required but is not published on the public register. The registered office address is public, which is the one people usually mean to ask about.

x.s: No US state formation document asks about your nationality. Not Wyoming's, not Delaware's, none of them. You can sit in Lagos or Lahore or Lisbon, file the paperwork a founder in Austin files, and the state will process it the same way.

A small industry exists to make US company formation sound like an immigration problem. It is not. Learning how to open a US LLC as a non resident is mostly learning which steps are trivial and which ones stop people. Formation is trivial. Banking and federal tax filing are the hard parts, and almost nobody says so up front.
There is no citizenship or residency requirement
Delaware's own FAQ is direct about it. The state requires a registered agent inside Delaware, and that requirement applies to the agent rather than to you. Delaware
explains it plainly
: no member or manager has to live in the state or the country. Other states work the same way.
You do not need a visa or to have ever entered the country. What forming a US LLC does not do is give you the right to live or work there. Ownership and immigration status are separate.
The registered agent requirement, and why a PO box fails
Every US state requires an LLC to name a registered agent with a physical street address in the state of formation, available during business hours to accept service of process.

Service of process means somebody hands your company a lawsuit. The state needs a real human at a real door to receive it, which is why a PO box does not satisfy the rule. A box in a mail room cannot be served and cannot sign for anything.

Your agent is also your default US mailing point, so state and IRS post lands there. Choose one that scans and forwards promptly, because losing agent status can put the company into bad standing. I am not quoting a price for this. The market ranges widely, there is no official figure, and numbers in comparison articles are usually affiliate deals.
Which state should you pick
Short version: pick a cheap, quiet state unless you have a specific reason not to.
Costs genuinely differ. Delaware charges
$110 to form
and a
$400 annual LLC tax
due 1 June, which rose from $300 this year and which most articles still get wrong. Wyoming charges
and a $60 a year minimum. California charges $70 and then
$800 a year
in franchise tax, and the first year waiver everyone mentions expired after 2023.
The full breakdown is in our comparison of
Wyoming, Delaware and New Mexico for LLC formation

. Two things to add. A cheap state of formation does not exempt you from registering where you actually operate, which only bites once you hire or rent somewhere. And Delaware's advantages are real for venture backed corporations and irrelevant to a bootstrapped LLC selling services online.
Getting the EIN without an SSN
An EIN is your company's federal tax number, and you cannot open a bank account or file the forms further down this page without one.

Here is the correction that saves people months. You do not need a Social Security Number or an ITIN. The IRS instructions for Form SS-4 say, at line 7b, to enter "foreign" or N/A if the responsible party does not have and cannot obtain either. The IRS online application will still refuse you, because it is closed to applicants with no US legal residence, principal place of business or principal office. That is a limitation of one web form, not a rule about eligibility.
International applicants apply by phone on
, which is not toll free, between 6:00 a.m. and 11:00 p.m. Eastern, Monday to Friday, or by fax or post using
Form SS-4
. The EIN is free. The full walkthrough is in
how to get an EIN without an SSN
The bank account is the part that actually stops people
Formation takes a day. The EIN takes a phone call. The bank account is where founders lose weeks and sometimes give up.
The regulation is on your side. FinCEN's customer identification rule at

says a bank may accept, from a person who is not a US person, a taxpayer identification number, or a passport number and country of issuance, or an alien identification card number. A passport is legally sufficient identification.

What blocks you is bank policy. Banks set requirements above the regulatory floor, and many want an SSN and a human standing in the branch. That is commercial, not legal, which is why identical paperwork gets different answers. Since no institution publishes a verifiable policy, I will not name one and tell you it says yes. What to prepare and what to ask is in
opening a US business bank account as a non resident LLC owner
Form 5472, and the $25,000 penalty nobody mentions
If your LLC has one owner and that owner is not a US person, the IRS treats it as a corporation for one narrow purpose: information reporting. You file a pro forma Form 1120 with
Form 5472
attached, whenever the company had a reportable transaction in the tax year.

Reportable transaction is broader than it sounds. It covers amounts paid or received in connection with the formation, acquisition and dissolution of the entity, including contributions to and distributions from it. Funding your own company's account counts, so a dormant LLC usually still has a filing obligation.

The penalty language is not ambiguous. A penalty of $25,000 is assessed on any reporting corporation that fails to file when due and in the manner prescribed, with a further $25,000 for each 30 day period beyond 90 days after IRS notification. Full detail is in
Form 5472 and the $25,000 penalty
BOI reporting is dead, and most articles have not caught up
Anything published before this year almost certainly tells you to file a beneficial ownership information report with FinCEN within 30 days of forming. Skip it.
FinCEN's
final rule of 11 August 2026

permanently removes the requirement for US companies and US persons to report beneficial ownership information under the Corporate Transparency Act, and FinCEN will delete information previously reported by US persons. An interim rule in March 2025 had already suspended it.
One nuance. A non US founder forming a new US LLC is covered, because the exemption follows the entity. A
foreign
company registering to do business in a US state is still a reporting company, so check that separately if it applies to you.

New Mexico's is repeated everywhere but I could not confirm it from a state source, so treat it as likely rather than certain. Agent and preparer fees have no published average, which is why those rows carry no number.
The honest version

Forming the company is the easy day. You will do it in an afternoon and wonder what the fuss was about. Then you will spend three weeks on a bank account, and discover in month eleven that there is a federal form nobody warned you about with a $25,000 penalty attached.

Anyone selling a package that ends at the state filing is selling you the easy day. Do it in this order: registered agent, state filing, EIN, bank account, calendar reminder for Form 5472. Get a US tax preparer before the first filing is due, not after.

items.q: Can a non US citizen own a US LLC?
items.a: Yes. No state imposes a citizenship or residency requirement on members or managers, and Delaware's guidance confirms the only in state requirement is a registered agent. You can own 100% of a US LLC without ever visiting the country. What ownership does not give you is any right to live or work there.

items.q: Do I need an ITIN before I can form a US LLC?
items.a: No, and this is the most expensive piece of bad advice in the category. You do not need an ITIN to form an LLC or to get an EIN. The IRS instructions for Form SS-4 explicitly allow a responsible party with no SSN or ITIN to write "foreign" on line 7b.

items.q: How long does it take to open a US LLC from abroad?
items.a: State filing is usually days, faster with expedited processing, and the EIN can be issued on a single phone call for international applicants. The bank account is the unpredictable part and takes days or weeks depending on the institution and how clearly you describe the business.

items.q: Do I still have to file a BOI report in 2026?
items.a: Not if you are forming a US entity. FinCEN's final rule of 11 August 2026 permanently ended the requirement for US companies and US persons. The exception is a foreign company registering to do business in a US state, which remains a reporting company. Any article telling you to file within 30 days of formation is out of date.

x.s: Most SOP examples for a small service business are written to look impressive rather than to be used. Twelve pages, a purpose statement, a scope statement, a revision history table, and no sentence saying what actually starts the thing.

A useful SOP is short and boring. It says what triggers it, who owns it, what the steps are in order, how you know it is finished, and what to do when it goes wrong. If a document has those five parts it works. If it is missing the trigger or the definition of done, it will sit unread in a shared drive forever.
Below are four SOPs written out in full, not described. Copy them, change the names, delete what does not apply.
What makes a useful SOP in a small service business
A trigger.
The observable event that starts it. "A form is submitted." "A deal moves to Won." Not "when a new client joins", which is a state, not an event.
An owner.
One named role. Not a team. If two people own it, nobody does.
Numbered steps.
In order, each one an action a person can do without asking a question. Say which tool, which field, which template.
A definition of done.
The condition that says it is finished. Everyone leaves this out, which is why work sits at ninety percent forever.
An escalation path.
What to do when reality does not match the steps.
Write in the imperative. "Send the welcome email", not "the welcome email should be sent".
SOP 1: New client onboarding
Trigger:
Deal moves to Won in the CRM.
Owner:
Account lead.
Done when:
The kickoff call has happened, the client has access to everything, and the project record shows a start date.

Create the client folder from the folder template, named for the client and start month.
Create the project record. Set the start date and the named client contact.
Send the intake form: billing contact, billing address, purchase order number if they use one,

items.s: Send the calendar link for the kickoff call. Offer three slots inside 10 business days.
Two business days before the call, confirm the intake form is complete. If not, phone the

x.s: client contact.

items.s: Run the kickoff call. Confirm scope, dates, the single point of contact on each side, and how

x.s: you will communicate.

items.s: Within 1 business day, send written notes with dates and owners.
Raise the deposit invoice per SOP 3.

the intake form is still incomplete 5 business days after kickoff, or the client asks for anything outside the signed scope. Escalate to the business owner, same day.

A website form submission, an email to the general inbox, or a voicemail.
Owner:
Whoever holds the enquiry inbox.

x.s: asked for.

items.s: Reply within 4 business hours on business days. Acknowledge what they asked for specifically,

If qualified, send the calendar link and set a CRM task for a call.
If not qualified, reply with a short honest no and a referral if you have one. Mark the record

x.s: Closed Lost with a reason.

the enquiry mentions a deadline inside 2 weeks, a budget above your normal range, or a legal or compliance requirement. Escalate to the business owner immediately.
SOP 3: Invoicing and chasing payment
One number first, because it changes how you write this one. Among US firms surveyed in three industrial sectors, Atradius found
43% of the value of B2B invoices was overdue

It is still good evidence that late payment is normal, so build chasing into the process rather than treating it as a surprise.
Trigger:
A milestone completes, or the invoicing date arrives for a retainer.
Owner:
Whoever runs the books.

Payment has cleared and the invoice is marked paid in the accounting system.

items.s: Raise the invoice within 1 business day. Include the purchase order number if the client uses

items.s: Send it to the billing contact captured at onboarding, not your day to day contact. Copy the

On day 1 overdue, email the billing contact and copy the day to day contact.
On day 7 overdue, phone. Email alone stops working around here.
On day 14 overdue, pause new work and say so in writing, referencing your contract.
On day 30 overdue, send a formal demand and decide whether to escalate.

SOP 4: Offboarding a client
The one everybody skips, and the one that costs most in security risk and lost referrals.
Trigger:
Final deliverable accepted, or notice given by either side.
Owner:
Account lead.
Done when:
Access is revoked, files are handed over, the final invoice is paid, and the CRM record is closed with an outcome.

items.s: Confirm the end date in writing and what is included before it.
Deliver everything outstanding. Send one handover document listing what was delivered and where.
Transfer ownership of assets held in your accounts: domains, ad accounts, analytics,

x.s: repositories.

items.s: Revoke your access to their systems and theirs to yours, within 5 business days.
Remove the client from internal automations and shared inboxes so nothing keeps firing.
Raise the final invoice per SOP 3.
Ask for a testimonial or referral 2 weeks after final delivery, not on the last day.
Set a CRM reminder to check in at 6 months.
Archive the folder and close the CRM record with an outcome note.

x.s: Escalate if:
the relationship ended badly, anything is disputed, or credentials cannot be recovered. Escalate to the business owner before sending anything further.
How to write SOP examples for your own business
Do not write SOPs for everything. Write them for what repeats and for what somebody else will eventually run.

The fastest method is to do the job once with a document open and narrate it. Write what you actually did, including the bit where you checked something in another tab. Then have someone else follow it and note every place they had to ask a question. Those are your missing steps.
Review each one when it fails, not on a schedule. A quarterly reminder gets ignored. A rule that says fix the document before you fix anything else does not.
Where this leads

An SOP is not a filing exercise. It is what lets you hand work to somebody else without two weeks of shadowing, and it is the prerequisite for automating anything. You cannot connect a set of tools to run a process nobody has written down.
That is the honest order of operations. Write it, run it manually until it stops surprising you, then look at what could run itself. Our guide to

items.q: What should a small business SOP include?
items.a: Five things: a trigger saying what starts it, one named owner, numbered steps in order, a definition of done, and an escalation path. Purpose statements, scope sections and revision tables are optional and mostly ignored. If it does not fit on one page, it is probably two SOPs pretending to be one.

items.q: How long should an SOP be?
items.a: One page. If a process needs more, split it, the way onboarding and invoicing are split above. Long documents get skimmed, and a skimmed SOP is worse than none because people believe they followed it. Screenshots help more than paragraphs when a step involves finding something in a tool.

items.q: Who should write the SOPs in a small business?
items.a: The person who currently does the job, not the owner writing down how they imagine it is done. The owner's version is always idealised. Have the person doing the work narrate it as they do it, then have a second person follow it and mark every point where they had to ask something.

items.q: Do I need SOPs before I automate anything?
items.a: Yes, and this is the practical reason to bother. Automation encodes a process exactly as written. If the process is not written, you will encode three people's different versions of it and find the conflict in production. Write the SOP, run it manually for a month, then automate the parts that never vary.

x.s: You will read a hundred times that you need a Social Security Number to open a US business bank account. It is not true, and the regulation that supposedly requires it says something close to the opposite.

That does not make this step easy. Getting a US business bank account as a non resident LLC owner is the part of the process that stops people, for a reason that has nothing to do with the law. It is bank policy. Every institution sets its own, none are published in comparable form, and two founders with identical paperwork routinely get different answers.

This article separates the rule from the policy, tells you what to have ready, and gives you the questions to ask before you spend a week on an application. It does not tell you which bank will say yes, because nobody can honestly tell you that.
What the regulation actually requires
The rule everyone is half remembering is FinCEN's Customer Identification Program requirement at
, which sets the minimum identifying information a bank must collect before opening an account.

For a person who is not a US person, the regulation lists what the bank may accept: "A taxpayer identification number; passport number and country of issuance; alien identification card number", or the number and country of issuance of any other government issued document that evidences nationality or residence and carries a photograph or similar safeguard.
Read the list. A passport number and country of issuance sits there as an alternative to a taxpayer identification number, not as a supplement to one.

So a passport is legally sufficient identification for a non US person opening an account. The regulation provides for exactly your situation. Any article saying federal law requires an SSN is describing a rule that does not exist.
Then why do banks keep saying no
Because the regulation is a floor, not a ceiling.

A bank is free to require more than the minimum, and most do. The reasons are commercial rather than legal. A customer who lives abroad, has no US credit history and cannot walk into a branch is harder to verify, harder to collect from, and more expensive to monitor.

So institutions build internal policies on top of the rule. Common ones include requiring an SSN or ITIN regardless of what the regulation permits, requiring the signer to appear in person at a branch, requiring a US residential address, or declining business accounts for entities with no US operations at all.

None of that is illegal. It is also not a legal requirement being passed on to you, even when the person at the counter says it is. Staff often believe the SSN rule is federal law, because it is the only version they have been trained on.
So a rejection is a policy outcome, not a verdict on your eligibility. The next institution may decide differently.
What to have ready before you apply
Assemble all of this before you start any application. Half prepared applications get abandoned, and abandoned applications sometimes leave a record.
Your EIN and the IRS confirmation.
No bank opens a business account without the company's federal tax number. It is free and you do not need an SSN to get it. Our guide to
getting an EIN without an SSN
covers the phone route for international applicants.
Formation documents.

The filed articles of organization or certificate of formation stamped by the state, plus a certificate of good standing if the state issues one. Some banks want a certified copy rather than a download.
Your operating agreement.
Signed, showing who owns the company and who has authority to open accounts and move money. Single owner companies often skip this. Do not skip it.
Registered agent details.
Name and full street address, since it is usually the company's address of record.
Your passport.
Valid, not close to expiry, and matching the name on every other document exactly. A middle name on one document and not another causes real delays.
Proof of address.
A recent utility bill or bank statement in your own name at your home address abroad. Recent usually means within three months.
A clear description of the business.
What you sell, to whom, in which countries, what volume you expect, and where the money comes from. Write it in two or three plain sentences first.

That last one matters more than founders expect. Compliance teams assess risk, and a vague answer reads as risk. "We provide software development services to agencies in the UK and Germany, invoiced monthly, expecting around ten transactions a month" gets a very different reception from "consulting".
The categories, and what to ask each one
Rather than name institutions and repeat approval claims nobody can verify, here are the categories and the questions that separate them. Ask before you apply, not after.

rows.s: National and regional banks with physical branches
Do you require the signer to appear in person, and do you require an SSN or ITIN for a foreign owner?
Business banking arms of larger institutions
Do you open accounts for US entities with no US physical presence or US resident officer?
Accounts opened online, often partnered with a chartered bank
Who actually holds the deposits, is it a bank or a payment institution, and are funds insured?
Multi currency accounts and payment rails
Is this a deposit account or a stored value balance, and what happens to my money if you close the account?

x.s: There is no source line under this table because there are no figures in it, deliberately. Approval rates, acceptance policies and country restrictions are not published in verifiable form, they change without notice, and every article that ranks providers is either guessing or being paid.

Two more questions worth asking anyone: what country restrictions apply to the owner's residence, and what triggers a review or closure later. The second is the one nobody asks and the one that hurts most, because an account that opens easily and closes six months into trading is worse than one that took three weeks to get.
Be honest about the odds
This is the step where people give up, and pretending otherwise does not help.

Approval is not guaranteed anywhere. No institution has a published policy of accepting every non resident LLC owner, and anyone promising a guaranteed US bank account is selling something. Expect several applications, at least one rejection, and a timeline in weeks rather than days.

What genuinely helps is unglamorous. Documents whose names match each other exactly. A business description a compliance officer understands in one read. An EIN already in hand rather than pending. A real website that describes the business, because compliance teams look, and an empty holding page is a red flag to somebody deciding whether you exist.
What does not help: applying to five providers at once, describing the business vaguely to avoid questions, or using an address you have no connection to.
Sequencing matters too. Form the entity, get the EIN, then approach banks. The full order is in
how to open a US LLC as a non resident
What this really comes down to
The law is not your problem. A passport is sufficient identification under the rule that actually governs this, and it has been for years.

Your problem is that you are applying to private companies that choose their own customers, whose policies are unpublished and inconsistent, and whose staff will explain those policies as if they were statutes. The strategy is to arrive very well prepared, ask the disqualifying questions before you invest time in an application, and accept that you may need more than one attempt.

website development
page covers that, and we are happy to talk the sequence through before you apply anywhere.

items.q: Do I need an SSN to open a US business bank account?
items.a: Not as a matter of law. The FinCEN customer identification rule at 31 CFR 1020.220 lets a bank accept a passport number and country of issuance from a person who is not a US person, as an alternative to a taxpayer identification number. What stops applications is individual bank policy, which frequently requires more than the regulation does.

items.q: Can I open a US bank account without visiting the United States?
items.a: Sometimes, depending entirely on the institution. Many traditional US branch banks require the signer to appear in person, which is a policy choice rather than a legal requirement. Providers built around online onboarding do not, though they set their own restrictions on owner residence and business type. Ask before you apply.

items.q: Do I need an EIN before opening the account?
items.a: Yes, in practice. Business accounts are opened in the company's name and the company's federal tax number is part of the identification the bank collects. The EIN is free and does not require an SSN or ITIN, and international applicants can get one on a single phone call to the IRS.

items.q: Why do banks say federal law requires a Social Security Number?
items.a: Usually because the person telling you believes it. Staff are trained on their employer's internal policy, and that policy often does require an SSN or ITIN, so it gets described as law. The underlying regulation is more permissive than the policies built on it, but the policy is what governs your application.

items.a: Keep records of every movement of money between you and the company. x.s: Most launch checklists are ordered by what is easy. Logo, name, Instagram handle, then around item fourteen, "register your business".

That ordering feels productive and wastes about two weeks, because what to do first when starting a business is not a question about priorities. It is a question about dependencies. You cannot open a business bank account without an EIN, cannot sensibly get an EIN without an entity, and cannot take a card payment into an account that does not exist. Four of your first steps are locked behind each other. The rest are not.

So here is a four week plan ordered by what unblocks the next thing, with the real US figures attached. Fair warning: a good chunk of week one is waiting on other people, and that is normal rather than a sign you did something wrong.

Day 3 to 7: apply for the EIN
The EIN is free. The IRS is unusually direct about it: "Beware of websites that charge for an EIN. You never have to pay a fee for an EIN."

Have every answer ready before you open the online application, because the session expires after 15 minutes of inactivity and restarts from the beginning. And if you have no legal residence, principal place of business or principal office in the United States, the online tool is closed to you. You apply by phone on 267 941 1099, not toll free, open 6:00 a.m. to 11:00 p.m. Eastern, Monday to Friday.

You do not need a Social Security Number for any of this. The IRS instructions say to enter "foreign" or N/A on line 7b when the responsible party has no SSN or ITIN and cannot get one. The common advice to obtain an ITIN first is wrong and costs people months, and we wrote it up in

The honest bit about week 1

Some of this week is dead time. State processing takes what it takes, mailed EIN applications take about four weeks, and no amount of energy changes either. Use the gap to draft your service descriptions and pricing, which nobody is holding up.
Week 2: banking and getting paid
Open the business account
Bring the formation documents, the EIN letter and your identification. For US owners this is routine.
For everyone else, the regulation is on your side even when the bank is not. Under FinCEN's Customer Identification Program rule,

, a bank may accept from a non US person a taxpayer identification number, or a passport number and country of issuance, or an alien identification card number, or another government issued document evidencing nationality or residence and bearing a photograph. A passport is legally sufficient. What blocks people is bank policy, not the rule, so the fix is choosing the right bank rather than chasing an SSN. Details in
opening a US bank account as a non resident
One filing to understand before money moves

If your LLC has a single owner who is not a US person, read this twice. Form 5472 applies to a foreign owned US disregarded entity that had any reportable transaction in the tax year, and that includes amounts paid or received in connection with the formation of the entity, including contributions to it. Funding your own account counts. The
IRS instructions

state that a penalty of $25,000 will be assessed on any reporting corporation that fails to file when due, with a further $25,000 for each 30 day period beyond 90 days after IRS notification. A dormant LLC almost always still has to file. Walkthrough in our
Form 5472 guide
One thing you can stop worrying about
Beneficial ownership reporting. FinCEN's final rule of 11 August 2026
permanently removed the requirement for US companies and US persons

to report beneficial ownership under the Corporate Transparency Act, and is deleting information already reported by US persons. Most launch checklists still list it as a step. It is not one, unless you are a foreign company registering to do business in a US state.
Set up invoicing before you need it
Pick something that produces a numbered invoice and takes a card. Do it this week rather than in the hour a client asks how to pay you.
Week 3: the customer facing layer
Now the website, and only the parts that matter in month one: what you do, who it is for, proof you exist, and a contact route that goes somewhere you check daily.
Then decide where an enquiry lives after it arrives. A spreadsheet is a legitimate answer for the first fifty leads. Enquiries sitting in an inbox with no owner and no next step are not. Our

Week 4: the operating layer
Write down the three things you will do most often. Not a manual, just the steps in order, with the link or template each one needs.

This is the week that decides whether the business can run without you at three months. It also makes the first hire survivable, because you hand over a document rather than a vibe. Worked examples in

Then look at what you repeated most this month and ask whether it needs a person at all.
The honest version of what to do first when starting a business
It is less dramatic than you expect and involves more waiting. A day on decisions, a week on forms, then several days refreshing an inbox for a letter from a state office.
The people who come out of month one in good shape are not the ones who worked hardest. They did the four locked steps in order, early, and used the dead time for the work nobody was blocking.

items.q: What should I do first when starting a business?
items.a: Form the entity and appoint a registered agent, because everything else is locked behind it. The EIN application asks for the legal entity name, and the bank asks for the EIN. Branding or a website first is not wrong, it just unblocks nothing, so it can happen while you wait on filings.

items.q: How long does it take to get an EIN?
items.a: Online it is immediate, issued at the end of the session. By fax it is generally within four business days. By mail it is approximately four weeks. International applicants who cannot use the online tool apply by phone and get it on the same call. Those are the IRS's published timelines.

items.q: Can I open a business bank account without an SSN?
items.a: Yes. The FinCEN customer identification rule allows a bank to accept a passport number and country of issuance from a non US person, among other documents. An SSN is not legally required. Banks apply stricter policies than the regulation demands, so the practical task is finding one whose policy is workable.

items.q: How much does the first month cost?
items.a: The unavoidable parts are small. A state filing fee between $50 and $425, a registered agent fee, and nothing for the EIN. Annual state costs start the clock immediately in some states, notably $800 a year in California and $400 in Delaware. Everything else is optional in month one.

items.q: What can I safely skip in the first 30 days?
items.a: The logo, the brand guidelines, the second landing page, and any tool you have not felt the absence of. None unblock anything. Skip them until something is actually waiting on them, which is usually later than it feels.

Three rows are worth stopping on, the ones published guides most often get wrong.
The Delaware $400 problem
Delaware's annual LLC tax is now $400, up from $300, following
legislation introduced in April 2026
. It is due June 1 every year, and it is flat rather than calculated on income, so a dormant Delaware LLC with no revenue owes the same $400 as a busy one.
If you are comparing states on a page written before this year, the Delaware column is understated by $100 a year, forever.
Delaware is still Delaware. Its Division of Corporations reports
more than 2.28 million registered entities, 334,461 new entities formed in 2025, over two thirds of the Fortune 500, and nearly 70% of US based IPOs in 2025
. A real ecosystem with real case law behind it. It is just not the cheap option, and for a two person consultancy it never was.
The California first year that is not free

Plenty of articles still tell you California waives the $800 franchise tax in your first year. That waiver applied only to tax years beginning 1 January 2021 through 31 December 2023, and it has expired. The
Franchise Tax Board
is the authority, and the current position is that the $800 annual minimum applies.

There is also an additional LLC fee once California source income crosses certain thresholds: $900 at $250,000, $2,500 at $500,000, $6,000 at $1,000,000, and $11,790 at $5,000,000 and above. Those sit on top of the $800.
That is why California has the most expensive recurring cost in the table despite one of the cheaper filing fees, and why so many people try to form somewhere else. Which brings us to the trap.
The New York cost nobody quotes
New York requires you, within 120 days of formation, to publish notice of your LLC in two newspapers designated by the county clerk, for six consecutive weeks, then file a
Certificate of Publication
for $50. Miss it and the LLC's authority to do business is suspended.

Here is the honest part. I cannot tell you what that costs, and neither can anyone else. The newspapers set the price, it varies enormously by county, and no official figure exists. Any article quoting a firm number for New York publication invented it or copied someone who did. Ask your county clerk which papers are designated, then get quotes from those papers.

New Mexico wins on paper, and it is also the one I would treat most carefully. The claim that it has no LLC annual report is repeated everywhere and I could not confirm it from a New Mexico state source. Ohio's equivalent claim is much better supported. Verify it with the Secretary of State before it becomes the reason you chose a state.
Wyoming is the sensible middle. A hundred dollars to file, sixty a year to maintain, or $0.0002 of your Wyoming located assets if that comes out higher, which for most remote businesses it will not.
Delaware costs five times what Wyoming costs each year. You pay that for a body of corporate law that investors and their lawyers already understand.
Wyoming vs Delaware vs New Mexico: when Delaware is worth it
If you are raising venture capital, you will almost certainly be told to be a Delaware C Corp, not an LLC in any state.

Worth being precise about why, because the way this gets repeated online is wrong. There is no rule requiring it. It is market practice, nothing more. The model financing documents the industry uses assume Delaware, the lawyers on both sides have done it a thousand times, and deviating means paying someone to think. That is a real cost and it is why the convention holds. But it is convention, not regulation, and if nobody is investing in you it does not apply.
The thing most of these comparisons leave out
Forming in Wyoming does not move your business to Wyoming.

If you live in California and run your business from California, forming an LLC in Wyoming generally means you are a Wyoming LLC doing business in California, which generally means registering in California as a foreign LLC as well. Two registered agents, two sets of filings, and California's $800 still lands. You have added cost and complexity, not removed it.
This is the most common expensive mistake in this topic. The state you actually operate in has its own view about businesses operating there, and that view usually wins.

So the practical rule for a normal small business, a shop, an agency, a contractor, a consultancy with local clients, is to form in the state you are in. Simpler, cheaper once you count both sides, and what your accountant would tell you.

These comparisons get interesting when you are a non US founder with no physical US presence, or an online business with no meaningful nexus anywhere. Then no home state is pulling you and picking on cost is reasonable. Our guide to
setting up a US LLC as a foreign founder
covers that.
What to do next
Work out where you actually do business first. Not where you would like to be taxed, where you have people, premises, inventory or regular clients.

If that is one state, form there and stop reading comparison articles. If it is genuinely nowhere, compare on the recurring column rather than the filing fee, because the filing fee happens once and the recurring cost happens forever.
Then budget for a registered agent, because one is mandatory everywhere.

If any of this touches multi state operations, employees in more than one place, or a serious tax question, ask a lawyer or a CPA licensed in that state. A hundred dollars of advice now is cheaper than unwinding a structure later.
The short version

If you run a business in a state, form it in that state. Everything else here is a distraction dressed up as optimisation, and the people selling you a Wyoming LLC rarely mention the second registration you will need at home.

items.q: Is Wyoming or Delaware better for an LLC?
items.a: For cost, Wyoming, and it is not close: $60 a year against Delaware's $400. For raising institutional investment, Delaware, though at that point you are usually forming a C Corp. If nobody is buying equity, the Delaware premium buys infrastructure you will never use.

items.q: Does New Mexico really have no annual report for LLCs?
items.a: That is the widely repeated claim and it may be correct, but I could not verify it from a New Mexico state source, so I will not assert it as fact. Treat it as probable rather than confirmed, and check with the Secretary of State first.

items.q: Can I form in Wyoming if I live in California?
items.a: You can form the entity there, but if you operate from California you will generally also need to register in California as a foreign LLC and pay the $800 annual franchise tax. You end up with two states instead of one. Ask a California CPA before doing it deliberately.

items.q: How much does the New York publication requirement cost?
items.a: Nobody can tell you, honestly. Newspapers set their own rates and the designated papers vary by county, so no official figure exists. Ask your county clerk which papers are designated, then get quotes from those papers before you form.
